title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate of paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We present the sealed design, execution accounting, representative examples, contamination‑check evidence (10% Mininet holdout → 20 tasks; contamination artifact reports zero disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational productivity gains but risks incorrect or unsafe changes that can cause outages, policy violations, or degraded service. Prior proposals therefore integrate LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) so that unsafe candidates can be detected and corrected before application. The operational value of automated repair depends on (i) the baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures produced by the chosen generator and prompt policy; (ii) the validator’s coverage and fidelity; and (iii) the repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We asked a narrowly scoped, preregistered confirmatory question: Does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank?

Contributions. (1) A sealed preregistered paired design (n = 200) that enforces shared‑initial generation semantics to isolate the marginal effect of applying a deterministic validator+repair to the same generated candidate. (2) An autonomous, fully archived execution with deterministic reconciliation and concrete accounting (completed pairs = 200, model_calls_used = 200, repair_calls = 0). (3) An honest, artifact‑grounded null/degenerate confirmatory outcome and interpretation clarifying when automated repair can and cannot reduce validator‑detected failures, together with operational recommendations and reproducibility notes grounded in archived artifacts.
sections.related_work: LLMs exhibit factual errors and prompt sensitivity across domains; mitigation approaches include grounding (retrieval augmentation), verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded/guarded agent architectures. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate intent→configuration synthesis is feasible, but published prototypes often omit instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate studies. Architectures that combine LLM generation with deterministic network validators (e.g., Batfish or domain checkers) and iterative repair loops have been proposed to improve safety; red‑team studies and configuration‑brittleness audits show tool‑description injection and cross‑tool ambiguity can materially change safety outcomes. Surveys and method papers call for externally auditable, preregistered measurements that isolate the marginal effect of adding deterministic repair for a fixed model and prompt policy. Our study sits among generator→validator→repair proposals and external‑evaluation critiques by measuring a prespecified paired estimand under tightly controlled, archived conditions using a curated task bank and a deterministic validator.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The experiment was preregistered as study id cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02. The frozen design required a paired binary comparison on a confirmatory sample of 200 tasks, a single pre‑registered primary test (exact McNemar two‑sided, α = 0.05), and an adapter‑enforced maximum model‑call cap of 400 (one initial generation per task plus up to one repair call if validation failed). The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Confidence intervals were computed with a bootstrap percentile method (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed a baseline unsafe incidence ≈ 30% and a target 50% relative reduction; the full preregistration and stopping rules were frozen before any model calls (preregistration SHA‑256: a9e5d64c...).

Task bank and validators. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks spanning four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Tasks encode initial and expected final states, workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group constraints) and an explicit required_sequence. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces task‑encoded constraints and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; the contamination artifact (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) records zero disagreements for that holdout.

Model, generation semantics, and adapter enforcement. The run used the hosted model declared in the preregistration (gpt‑5‑mini) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Crucially, the adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single initial candidate (deterministic sampling policy) which was then reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This design isolates the effect of validator+repair on the same generator output and removes per‑condition sampling variance that could otherwise confound paired inference. Adapter accounting shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming shared reuse across conditions.

Repair policy, budgets, and contamination handling. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM per task when the primary validator reported violations; up to 200 repair calls were therefore allowed but only if initial candidates failed validation. The contamination_plan deterministically excluded tasks where primary validator vs emulator disagreed; sensitivity analyses to treat flagged tasks as failures or successes were preregistered. Missingness/exclusion rules and the treatment of technical failures were fixed before execution. All design choices, seeds, model calls, validator diagnostics and logs were archived in the execution bundle for audit.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcome. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions) and complete_pair_count = 200. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) show baseline successes = 200/200 and guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Primary inferential result. With zero discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the prespecified ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is untestable on this sample because there were no baseline validator failures for GVR to reduce.

Repair activity, contamination check, and provider accounting. Because no initial candidate failed deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the GVR pipeline applied zero repair prompts and incurred zero repair‑call cost. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed and the contamination artifact (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) reports zero validator–emulator disagreements. Provider auditing shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, cache_hit_count = 0, reflecting one generator invocation per task that was deterministically reused across conditions.

Representative examples and diagnostics. Representative task artifacts (pair‑000001 through pair‑000006) show initial generator outputs that matched the task required_sequence and passed validation: validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0 in each representative record. Difficulty annotations (e.g., make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) and parsed_command_count/required_command_count confirm tasks exercised medium‑to‑very_hard workflow constraints even though generator outputs satisfied deterministic checks.

Planned sensitivity branches not invoked. The preregistration included sensitivity analyses for flagged contamination and alternative missingness treatments; because no tasks were flagged and no episodes failed, these branches were not executed. Secondary estimands (average repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) remain unpopulated in the analysis bundle because no repair attempts occurred.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation and operational meaning. The observed degenerate confirmatory outcome demonstrates a logical point: when a chosen model, prompt policy, and adapter produce validator‑passing candidates for all items in a workload, a validator‑coupled repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. This null result is tightly scoped: it does not imply GVR is never useful. Instead, it shows GVR’s marginal operational benefit is conditional on baseline validator failure prevalence and on validator coverage. Organizations should therefore measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workload distributions before investing heavily in automated repair automation.

Why baseline failures were zero on this bank. Artifact‑grounded explanations include: (1) the prompt template and the deterministic shared_initial semantics produced candidates that conformed to explicit task bank constraints; (2) the curated task bank encodes workflows with explicit required_sequences mapping directly to validator checks, making them easier for a correctly prompted generator to satisfy; (3) the primary validator enforces those encoded constraints but may omit device‑level or vendor idiosyncratic behaviors only visible under end‑to‑end execution; and (4) the single repair budget combined with shared_initial design removes per‑condition re‑sampling as a path to generate alternative, repairable candidates.

Implications for evaluation design. Confirmatory tests of GVR should be based on workload samples that exhibit nontrivial baseline validator failure rates under the chosen generator/prompt policy; otherwise the marginal effect is mechanically zero. Practical study designs to reveal GVR value include (a) adversarial or stressed task distributions that expose validator coverage gaps, (b) multi‑sample per‑condition generation to allow repairs that derive from alternative candidate draws, (c) multi‑step repair budgets, and (d) richer validator models that incorporate device/emulator semantics.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: preregistration, deterministic adapter enforcement, and frozen stopping rules guard against post‑hoc design changes; but the shared_initial design intentionally trades external generality for internal control. Construct validity: the primary validator enforces declared syntactic and intent constraints but may not capture all real device failure modes (emulator or real device signals may reveal additional faults). External validity: evaluation used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), one sampling policy (shared_initial, deterministic), and a curated task bank; results may differ across model families, nonzero temperature sampling, per‑condition independent draws, larger repair budgets, or adversarially drawn workloads. Conclusion validity: exact McNemar inference is uninformative with zero discordant pairs; nevertheless reporting the zero‑discordance outcome is evidence about baseline generator behavior and validator coverage on the selected workload.

Operational recommendations. Before deploying automated repair, measure baseline validator failure prevalence and validator–emulator agreement on representative workloads; if baseline failures are rare, improve validator fidelity (add device semantics, vendor idiosyncrasies), exercise adversarial tests, or consider multi‑sample generation and/or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals to create actionable repair opportunities. When baseline failures are nontrivial, GVR can reduce validator‑detected issues; realized gains depend on repair budget, repair prompt engineering, and validator completeness.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was not testable on this task bank because the baseline failure rate was 0%. The result emphasizes that the marginal value of automated repair is workload dependent: when baseline validator failures are rare, repair yields no measured benefit for validator‑detected errors. Future work should evaluate GVR on workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, extend validator fidelity with richer emulator or device checks, evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model generation policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize practical operational gains. All execution artifacts, logs, and analysis outputs are archived for independent inspection.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02 and used the hosted model declared as gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and the deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). The primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the contamination artifact (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) reports zero disagreements. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls (preregistration SHA‑256: a9e5d64cbe3a888170d614b971313b4f1550707d39db945843bca930d8caf5d6). Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
